intuition: Keep a pointer to the node before the next node you will inspect. If that next node has the unwanted value, skip it by changing the link. Otherwise, move forward. A dummy node before the head makes removing the first node work in the same way.

A dummy before the head makes even the first real node a deletable next neighbor. At every iteration, inspect prev.next. If it matches val, bypass it and leave prev in place; otherwise retain it and move prev forward. The link rewrite itself consumes the deleted node.

The retained prefix never contains a forbidden value, and each step handles one unprocessed node. This keeps the original surviving nodes and their relative order without allocating a second list. The dummy also handles an empty result uniformly.

steps: For [1,2,6,3,4,5,6] and val=6, begin with prev=dummy.
Node 1 is retained, so prev moves to 1. Node 2 is retained next, moving prev to 2.
The next node is 6. Redirect node 2.next to node 3 and leave prev at node 2.
Inspect the new next neighbor, node 3. Retain it, then retain nodes 4 and 5 in the same way.
At node 5, the final next neighbor is 6. Bypass it, making node 5.next=None.
The loop ends because no neighbor remains. Returning dummy.next yields the retained chain [1,2,3,4,5].

codeNotes.note: The next node is the unprocessed candidate, while prev is always the node that owns the link being changed.
Deletion exposes a new candidate without moving prev. This is why consecutive matching nodes are handled correctly.
Advance only after retaining the neighbor. The invariant then extends the clean prefix by exactly one node.

keyDecision: After removing a node, do not advance the previous pointer: the new next node still needs checking.

concept.question: How can one predecessor bookmark remove even several adjacent unwanted nodes?
intuition: Deleting the current node without its predecessor makes head deletion and consecutive deletions awkward. The incoming link is what must change.

Add a temporary starting node before the head. Inspect the node after the predecessor bookmark. If it is unwanted, bypass it while keeping the predecessor fixed; otherwise advance to that retained node.
concept.observation: After a removal, stay at the predecessor and inspect its new successor.
approach: Place a temporary node before the head.
Bypass unwanted successors, keeping the predecessor fixed.
Advance only when retaining a successor, then return the first real node.
concept.correctness: The predecessor’s completed prefix contains exactly the retained original nodes in order. Bypassing an unwanted successor extends inspection without adding it; advancing over a wanted successor extends the retained prefix. Repeating these actions examines every node and leaves exactly the desired chain.

complexity.explanation: Every node is inspected once. One temporary node and a bookmark use constant extra memory; work is linear.

pitfalls: After a removal, stay at the predecessor and inspect its new successor.
Return the temporary start’s final successor.
